name: Infinitival To Stranding

1.definition: Realizes an infinitival complement with overt to and a contextually recoverable predicate.

examples.form: I didn’t go, but I [wanted to].

projection.target: To can remain in the position where the full infinitival would occur. The same speaker can recover go without substituting lexical do so.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Ending a sentence with to
curious.summary: After words like wanted, the word to can stand without a verb after it when the listener can work out what verb is meant.
curious.body:
In I didn't go, but I wanted to, the sentence stops at to. You know the missing verb is go, because it was just mentioned. The to stays where a full phrase such as to go would have been.

This lets a speaker avoid repeating a verb. It's a different way of recovering the meaning from using do so in its place.

examples.text: I didn’t go, but I [wanted to].
She asked me to help, and I'm happy [to].

curious.try: Say I wanted to go, then say it again, dropping go. What does the listener supply?

teacher.summary: Explains to with an unexpressed verb phrase, as in I wanted to.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an infinitival complement realized with overt to and a contextually recoverable predicate. In I didn't go, but I wanted to, to stays in the position where the full infinitival would occur, and the listener recovers go from context. The same speaker can recover go without substituting lexical do so. This dictionary relates the pattern to the do so anaphor and marks it provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called VP ellipsis after to or a stranded to. This dictionary describes it as a to-infinitival with an unexpressed verb phrase.

examples.text: I didn’t go, but I [wanted to].
She asked me to help, and I'm happy [to].

contrasts.text: I didn't go, but I wanted to.
contrasts.note: To stranded; go recovered from context.

contrasts.text: I didn't go, but I wanted to go.

watch_for: A learner might think a sentence ending in to is unfinished.
A learner might look for a verb after to in the same clause rather than recovering it from context.
teacher.activity: Students read short exchanges with a stranded to and write what verb the listener recovers. They then repeat the exchange with the full infinitival.

child.hook: Can a sentence end with the word "to"?
child.explain: Sometimes a sentence ends with to, and you still know the verb. I didn't go, but I wanted to. You know the missing word is go.

examples.text: I didn’t go, but I [wanted to].
Mia asked me to play, and I [wanted to].

child.play: Tell a partner something you didn't do but wanted to, like I didn't swim, but I wanted to. Stop after to. Can your partner say the missing verb?

checked.note: Fixed: child game rewritten as one concrete step (say something you didn't do but wanted to, stopping at to, with an example that gives the partner the verb). Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary' in teacher text.
